relevance_reason: The study defines a peripheral-blood DNA methylation episignature for JARID2-neurodevelopmental syndrome (DIDDF). It uses 8 patients with pathogenic or likely pathogenic JARID2 variants, and tests 3 patients with variants of uncertain significance against the signature.

findings.statement: Verberne et al. (2022) described JARID2 haploinsufficiency as causing a neurodevelopmental syndrome. It is characterized by developmental delay, cognitive impairment ranging from borderline intellectual functioning to severe intellectual disability, hypotonia, autistic features, and behavior abnormalities. Dysmorphic facial features include a high anterior hairline, broad forehead, deeply set eyes, infraorbital dark circles, depressed nasal bridge, bulbous nasal tip, and full lips.
quotes: JARID2 (Jumonji, AT Rich Interactive Domain 2; OMIM 601594) haploinsufficiency has been associated with a clinically distinct neurodevelopmental syndrome. It is characterized by developmental delay, cognitive impairment (ranging from borderline intellectual functioning to severe intellectual disability), hypotonia, autistic features and behavior abnormalities.
Dysmorphic facial features include high anterior hairline, broad forehead, deeply set eyes, infraorbital dark circles, depressed nasal bridge, bulbous nasal tip and full lips.

findings.statement: Verberne et al. (2022) summarized 8 patients with pathogenic or likely pathogenic JARID2 variants: 4 males and 4 females aged 5 to 36 years, 5 of whom had been reported previously. All 8 had developmental delay. Intellectual functioning ranged from normal (1 patient) through learning difficulties or borderline functioning to moderate ID. Other features were autistic features (4 of 8, 2 with an ASD diagnosis), behavior abnormalities (3), hypotonia (2), gait disturbance (2), and variable facial dysmorphism. Additional anomalies included submucous cleft palate with bifid uvula, cryptorchidism, an arachnoid cyst or posterior fossa cyst/mega cisterna magna, kyphoscoliosis, and cafe-au-lait macules.

findings.statement: Verberne et al. (2022) reported 6 patients with deletions of at least one exon of JARID2 on chromosome 6p22.3, identified by microarray analysis or other methods. Five deletions were de novo. Patient 6 inherited her deletion from her mother (patient 7), who had learning difficulties.
quotes: Eight patients carried a pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant, including six patients with a deletion of at least one exon of JARID2, one patient with a frameshift variant and one with a splice site variant.
Patients 6 and 7 have the same deletion and are related (mother and daughter).

findings.statement: Verberne et al. (2022) reported a 14-year-old boy (patient 4) with moderate ID, autism spectrum disorder, and behavior abnormalities. He carried a de novo heterozygous frameshift variant in JARID2, c.2866dupG (p.Glu956GlyfsTer72), which was classified as pathogenic.
quotes: c.2866dupG p.(Glu956GlyfsTer72)

findings.statement: Verberne et al. (2022) reported a 5-year-old boy (patient 5) with developmental delay, hypotonia, an arachnoid cyst, right cryptorchidism, and congenital torticollis. He carried a de novo heterozygous splice site variant in JARID2, c.2731+1G-C, which was classified as likely pathogenic.

Verberne et al. (2022) analyzed peripheral blood DNA methylation (EPIC arrays) in 8 patients with pathogenic or likely pathogenic JARID2 variants and 56 matched controls. They identified a 150-probe episignature that clearly separated patients from controls on hierarchical clustering and multidimensional scaling, and the signature held up in leave-one-out cross-validation. A support vector machine classifier gave all patients scores near 1 and gave controls and samples from 57 other disorders low scores, which the authors interpreted as full sensitivity and specificity.
quotes: Our three-step feature selection procedure yielded 150 probes (Tables S1 and S2) with which we observed a clear clustering of patients and controls, based on hierarchical clustering and MDS visualizations.

All the samples with (likely) pathogenic JARID2 variants received MVP scores near 1, while all the control samples and case samples from other neurodevelopmental disorders received low MVP scores. Therefore, we conclude that our model has full sensitivity and specificity.

findings.statement: Verberne et al. (2022) tested 3 patients with JARID2 missense variants of uncertain significance against the episignature. Two unrelated patients (9 and 11) carried c.2363G-A (p.Arg788Gln); in patient 11 it was maternal, from an apparently unaffected mother. Patient 10 carried a de novo c.1930G-A (p.Glu644Lys) in the ARID domain. All 3 clustered with controls and had scores near zero. The authors noted this did not rule out pathogenicity but suggested the variants might be benign: patients 9 and 10 lacked the typical facial dysmorphism, and patient 11 had severe global spasticity and lack of myelination.
quotes: The three patients with JARID2 VUSs were also supplied into the model and received MVP scores near zero, indicating the dissimilarity of their methylation profile to the identified JARID2-neurodevelopmental syndrome episignature (Figure 5).
we think that these JARID2 missense variants might very well be benign variants and that the phenotype of these patients is caused by another, currently unknown, genetic aberration.

findings.statement: Verberne et al. (2022) found no significant differentially methylated regions. Among the 150 episignature probes, they found 7 small regions with a consistent direction of effect. Two of these were annotated to genes previously linked to abnormal neurological development, NLGN2 and ADGRL2. Gene set enrichment did not identify consistent pathways.
quotes: However, two of these seven regions were annotated to genes previously linked with aberrant neurological development. First, the NLGN2 gene previously was associated with autism and pervasive developmental disorders. Secondly, the ADGRL2 (LPHN2) gene was previously associated with a mild brain malformation (rhombencephalosynapsis).

relevance_reason: Case series reporting additional patients with JARID2 variants causing DIDDF, expanding phenotype and showing inheritance with variable expressivity.

findings.statement: Cadieux-Dion et al. (2022) reported 7 individuals from 5 families with pathogenic or likely pathogenic JARID2 variants, which confirmed the gene-disease association. The cases highlighted palatal abnormalities and heart defects as part of the phenotype.
quotes: Here, we present seven additional individuals from five families with pathogenic or likely pathogenic JARID2 variants, confirming this gene-disease association and highlighting palatal abnormalities and heart defects as part of the phenotype.

findings.statement: Cadieux-Dion et al. (2022) reported that JARID2 variants were inherited from mildly affected parents, which demonstrated variable expressivity of the disorder.
quotes: In addition, we report inheritance of JARID2 variants from mildly affected parents, demonstrating the variable expressivity of the disease.

findings.statement: Cadieux-Dion et al. (2022) noted a high prevalence of intragenic JARID2 copy number variants among the patients and emphasized the importance of exon-level analysis.
quotes: We also note the high prevalence of intragenic JARID2 copy number variants, emphasizing the importance of exon-level analysis.

relevance_reason: This paper reports 16 individuals from 15 families who have JARID2 deletions or single-nucleotide variants and developmental delay or intellectual disability. On that basis it defines the JARID2 haploinsufficiency syndrome (DIDDF).

findings.statement: Verberne et al. (2021) concluded that JARID2 haploinsufficiency causes a clinically distinct neurodevelopmental syndrome. Its features are developmental delay and/or intellectual disability and characteristic facial features.
quotes: We report that JARID2 haploinsufficiency leads to a clinically distinct neurodevelopmental syndrome, thus establishing gene-disease validity for the purpose of diagnostic reporting.

findings.statement: Verberne et al. (2021) reported 16 individuals from 15 families who had a deletion or single-nucleotide variant in JARID2. All had developmental delay and/or intellectual disability. They shared some clinical features, such as facial features, with individuals who have larger 6p22-p24 deletions that include JARID2.
quotes: We report 16 individuals in 15 families with a deletion or single-nucleotide variant in JARID2.
All individuals have developmental delay and/or ID and share some overlapping clinical characteristics such as facial features with those who have larger deletions involving JARID2.

findings.statement: Verberne et al. (2021) used chromosome microarray analysis, exome sequencing and GeneMatcher to find deletions or single-nucleotide variants involving JARID2 in 16 individuals from 15 families. The authors suggested that several of the variants were likely to cause haploinsufficiency through nonsense-mediated mRNA decay.
quotes: Chromosome microarray analysis, exome sequencing, and an online matching platform (GeneMatcher) were used to identify individuals with single-nucleotide variants or deletions involving JARID2.
Several of these variants are likely to result in haploinsufficiency due to nonsense-mediated messenger RNA (mRNA) decay.

findings.statement: Verberne et al. (2021) noted that 13 previously reported individuals with intellectual disability had de novo heterozygous 6p22-p24 deletions that removed all of JARID2. Every one of these deletions also removed at least one neighbouring gene, so it could not be determined whether JARID2 was the critical gene.
quotes: So far, 13 individuals sharing clinical features including intellectual disability (ID) were reported with de novo heterozygous deletions in 6p22-p24 encompassing the full length JARID2 gene (OMIM 601594).
However, all published individuals to date have a deletion of at least one other adjoining gene, making it difficult to determine if JARID2 is the critical gene responsible for the shared features.

relevance_reason: Only the abstract was available. It reports that an exon 6 CNV in JARID2, a gene the authors describe as known to cause ID, is benign, with a population frequency above 14%. This is useful context for interpreting variants in this entry. Most of the paper is about other epigenetic regulatory genes.

findings.statement: Zahir et al. (2016) had earlier found a CNV involving only exon 6 of the JARID2 gene, apparently de novo, in 7 patients with intellectual disability. JARID2 exon 6 encodes one of a series of repeated motifs, so the authors studied this variant in 2 cohorts and carried out a genotype-phenotype assessment. They concluded that the JARID2 exon 6 CNV is benign, with a high population frequency (more than 14%), although it could still have a contributory effect.
quotes: Previously, we found a CNV involving only exon 6 of the JARID2 gene occurred apparently de novo in seven patients. JARID2 is known to cause ID and other neurodevelopmental conditions.
We find the JARID2 exon 6 CNV is benign, with a high population frequency (>14%), but nevertheless could have a contributory effect.

variants.as_reported: CNV involving only exon 6 of the JARID2 gene

relevance_reason: Reports 4 patients with de novo 6p22.3 deletions including JARID2 (one deleting only part of JARID2 and DTNBP1) with a shared phenotype of developmental delay/ID, gait disturbance, and characteristic facial dysmorphism, and proposes JARID2 haploinsufficiency as the cause; there is no point mutation evidence.

findings.statement: Barøy et al. (2013) described 4 unrelated patients (2 females aged 15 and 6.5 years, 2 males aged 4 and 6.5 years; 3 Norwegian or Norwegian/English, 1 Lebanese, all of nonconsanguineous parents) with de novo 6p22.3 deletions including JARID2. All 4 had developmental delay with cognitive impairment ranging from borderline IQ to severe intellectual disability, gait disturbance with impaired balance and coordination, and similar facial dysmorphic features. These included prominent supraorbital ridges, deep-set eyes, dark infraorbital circles, midface hypoplasia, bulbous nasal tip, full lips, marked Cupid's bow, and a prominent or pointed chin. Other features were clinodactyly of the fifth fingers and foot anomalies such as syndactyly of toes, along with seizures or seizure-suspected episodes in 2 patients, behavioral abnormalities in 3, autism spectrum disorder in 1, and an atrial septal defect in 1.
quotes: JARID2 haploinsufficiency is likely to be the main contributor to the neurodevelopmental syndrome in Patients 1–4 consisting of impaired cognitive function, gait disturbance and distinct, similar dysmorphic facial features characterized by prominent supraorbital ridges, deep set eyes, dark infraorbital circles and midface hypoplasia.

findings.statement: Barøy et al. (2013) reported a 6.5-year-old Lebanese boy (Patient 4) of nonconsanguineous parents who had the smallest JARID2-containing deletion. He walked at 16 months and had language delay of 1.5 years at age 4 years 3 months, and his IQ was 74 (borderline) at 6.5 years. He had balance and coordination problems, poor finger opposition, and early-onset muscular hypotonia; neuromuscular and metabolic workups were normal, and cerebral MRI and EEG were normal. He had the characteristic facial features, strabismus, fifth-finger clinodactyly, syndactyly of toes 2-3, sandal gap, and broad halluces.
quotes: Testing with WPPSI-III at age 6.5 years gave a borderline IQ of 74 (borderline intellectual functioning: IQ 70–84).

He had balance and coordination problems (Additional file 6: Video Patient 4). Finger opposition was inadequate and he performed poorly when asked to stand on one leg at a time, jump, or walk on his toes or heals.

findings.statement: In a cohort of about 3,600 patients ascertained for neurodevelopmental disorders, Barøy et al. (2013) used aCGH to identify de novo 6p22.3-p24.1 deletions in 5 patients. Deletions in 4 patients, ranging from 189 kb to 4.8 Mb, shared a smallest region of overlap (SRO I) of 189 kb that included JARID2 and DTNBP1. This region was defined by the 189-kb deletion in Patient 4, which removed exons 3 to 18 and the 3-prime UTR of JARID2 and exons 7 to 10 of DTNBP1. Parental testing showed that all deletions were de novo, and DGV contained only CNVs covering minor parts of the region.
quotes: In Patient 4, we identified a 189–241 kb deletion, including part of the genes JARID2 and DTNBP1, which was the region defining SRO I, deleted in Patients 1–4.
deleting exons 3–18 in JARID2, exons 7–10 in DTNBP1 and exons 8–9 in ATXN1 and the 3’ untranslated region (UTR) in all cases.
were found to be de novo by aCGH analysis of the parental samples.

variants.as_reported: 189–241 kb deletion, including part of the genes JARID2 and DTNBP1 (exons 3–18 of JARID2)

findings.statement: Barøy et al. (2013) found that JARID2 expression in leukocyte RNA was significantly lower in the 4 patients with JARID2 deletion than in 8 healthy controls (p ≤ 0.01). They argued against DTNBP1 as the causal gene and concluded that JARID2, a transcriptional repressor and chromatin modifier acting in the PRC2 and Notch pathways, was likely the critical gene within SRO I.
quotes: JARID2 expression was significantly reduced in our patients compared to controls (p ≤ 0.01) (Figure 4A).
Thus a link between DTNBP1 haploinsufficiency and the features seen in our patients is unlikely.
we suggest that JARID2 is likely to be the critical gene within SRO I, and the main gene causing the neurodevelopmental syndrome in Patients 1–4.

findings.statement: Barøy et al. (2013) reviewed 10 previously reported patients with deletions including JARID2. The characteristic facial features were not consistently reported in these patients, but inspection of photographs available for 7 of them confirmed a similar facial pattern. Four of the 10 had impaired balance, impaired coordination, and/or gait disturbance. The authors suggested that JARID2 haploinsufficiency may result in a clinically recognizable neurodevelopmental syndrome and recommended sequencing JARID2 in similar patients without a deletion.
quotes: These features were not consistently reported in the 10 previously described patients with JARID2 deletion (Patients 1, 3, 6 from, A, C-G and J, Table 2 and Figure 3), but when we carefully inspected the photos available for seven of these individuals, a similar facial pattern could be confirmed.
Impaired balance and coordination and/or gait disturbance were noted in four out of the 10 previously reported patients with JARID2 deletion
we suggest that this gene should be sequenced in future patients with a similar phenotype when a gene deletion is not present.

findings.statement: Barøy et al. (2013) observed that Patient 5, a 17-year-old Norwegian girl with a de novo 116-kb deletion including GMPR and part of ATXN1 but not JARID2, had mild intellectual disability and behavioral abnormalities without the facial dysmorphism or gait disturbance. Patients 1 to 3, whose deletions included both JARID2 and ATXN1, had moderate to severe intellectual disability. The authors suggested that simultaneous deletion of both genes likely exacerbated the degree of intellectual disability.
quotes: A 116–163 kb deletion was detected in Patient 5 including the gene GMPR and part of the gene ATXN1.
Simultaneous deletion of the two genes likely exacerbated the degree of intellectual disability in three of our patients.
